summary: This FYI memo answers the question what is the Internet, and was produced by the User Services Working Group of the IETF. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This paper answers a simple question, what is the Internet, for people who were hearing about it for the first time.

questions: fyi on what is the internet
subtitle: A 1993 FYI that answers a surprisingly hard question: what exactly is the Internet?

tldr.problem: People often ask what the Internet is, and there is no single agreed answer that neatly sums it up.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives several definitions, then reprints an updated chapter from Ed Krol's 1992 book covering history, makeup, governance, funding and the outlook.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational snapshot of the Internet as understood in 1993, including open issues such as growth, commercialization and privatization.

today: RFC 1462 is an Informational FYI memo, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It describes the Internet as of May 1993, so its figures and open issues are historical.

sections.title: What Is the Internet?
sections.content:
The memo, an FYI produced by the IETF User Services Working Group, starts by admitting there is no agreed answer. The Internet can be seen through its common protocols, as a physical collection of routers and circuits, as a set of shared resources, or as an attitude about interconnection. Common definitions are a network of networks based on TCP/IP, a community of people, and a collection of reachable resources.

It began as an experiment by the U.S. Department of Defense over 20 years earlier. The networks share a standard set of protocols but also have gateways to networks running other protocols.
sections.eli5: Nobody agrees on one short answer. The Internet is wires and computers, people, and information, all at once.

sections.title: How the Internet Grew
sections.content:
The Internet began by connecting the ARPAnet with other radio and satellite networks. The ARPAnet was designed to survive partial outages, so the network was assumed to be unreliable and the computers at the ends were responsible for making sure communication worked. A computer only had to put its data in an IP packet and address it correctly.

IP software spread to every kind of computer, and with Ethernet LANs and workstations from around 1983, sites wanted to connect whole local networks. The National Science Foundation created five supercomputer centers and built NSFNET on 56,000 bit per second lines, then regional networks to save on line costs. When traffic overloaded it, a 1987 contract went to Merit Network with IBM and MCI, and the new network used lines faster by a factor of 20. NSF funded campus connections only if the campus had a plan to spread access around.
sections.eli5: A network built to keep working even if parts broke got joined by more and more networks. When the roads got crowded, they built bigger ones.

sections.title: What Makes Up the Internet
sections.content: The memo says the answer changes over time. Five years earlier it would have been all the IP networks that cooperate as a seamless whole: federal, regional, campus and some foreign networks. Since then, non-IP networks such as Bitnet and DECnets have connected through gateways, at first only to move electronic mail and later to translate other services. Whether they are part of the Internet depends on whether they want to be.
sections.eli5: Some networks that speak a different language connect through translators. Whether they count as part of the Internet depends on whether they want to belong.

sections.title: Governance and Funding
sections.content:
The Internet has no president or single authority. The memo gives ultimate authority to the Internet Society (ISOC), a voluntary membership organization, which appoints the Internet Architecture Board (IAB). The IAB blesses standards, sets rules for unique numbers such as the 32-bit address, and does not itself assign addresses. The IETF meets to discuss operational and near-term technical problems and creates working groups, whose reports may become documentation, voluntary practice or a standard sent to the IAB.

No one pays for the Internet as a whole. The NSF pays for NSFNET and NASA pays for the NASA Science Internet. A college or corporation pays a regional network, which pays a national provider. Each network has its own network operations center that talks to the others, much like telephone carriers.
sections.eli5: No one owns the whole Internet. Each group looks after and pays for its own piece, and they cooperate when something breaks.

sections.title: Open Issues in 1993
sections.content:
The memo lists several issues. ISO/OSI had become an international standard, but the authors saw no real advantage in moving to it, calling it more complex and less mature than IP. The Internet was in over 50 countries, with RIPE coordinating Europe since 1989 and about 25% of hosts located there. Poor telephone systems limited some regions to 9600 bits/second.

Commercialization was expected to grow as restrictions on commercial use were reviewed. Privatization, with telephone companies offering IP connections, faced obstacles around funding for existing connections, especially for schools.
sections.eli5: The Internet was spreading to more countries and businesses, and people were asking whether private companies, not the government, should run it.
